I'd venture to guess that the logical conclusion to self-driving cars would be self-driving flying cars. One of the major barriers to flying cars is the human element. Once that is circumvented, it becomes remarkably easier to create flying personal craft for the layperson.

It probably just seemed like the natural progression at the time. Writers of the past probably thought: "Driving is better than walking, and everyone owns a car that they use to go places, right? Well, last week I took a trip on Pan-Am and flying is better than driving. So, that means that in the future everyone will own a flying car that they use to fly places!"

In general terms, a lot of sci fi tropes are not revolutionary - but evolutionary. Flight is pretty obvious. The first helicopter designed on record is credited to DaVinci from the 1400s. He called it a flying screw. Introduce massive scale industrialization + price reduction - which again is something that these sci fi authors were familiar with, and a flying car sounds more or less like an inevitability.

Computational power on the other hand is something still incredibly new. Think about the fact that computers did not exist in the 30s. The first computer was the ENIAC, completed in 1946. It occupied 1800 square feet of space. And it had a computational power millions of times less than what your phone today has. Imagining going from those monstrosities to things just an inch or so in size, with performance millions of times greater. And with prices so low that they'd be used in just about everything with every person in a developed nation having access to them. That sounds a lot more far fetched than a flying car.

It'd be kind of like today imagine spaceships or cars capable of being driven by engines that are one square inch in size - and cost the equivalent a hundred bucks. Just seems like something that you'd be more inclined to call fantasy than sci-fi. Getting to where we are today required revolutionary, rather than evolutionary, progress. The hardware in computers today has little to nothing in common with with the hardware of the ENIAC. By contrast combustion engine cars today are much improved, but still use the exact same fundamental technology as the first production car released more than a century ago. However, the swap to pure electric engines has started a true revolution in how automobiles are powered - and one can only imagine where that will take us in the decades to come.
